tagline: Electric fields create a twist - not a push
audio_script: Here is the surprising part: an electric field can make an object rotate even when the total force is zero. Imagine a tiny dipole, with plus and minus charges separated by a distance. The field pushes the positive charge one way and the negative charge the other way. Those forces cancel as a net force, but because they act at different points, they create a torque. The torque is p E sine theta. So the dipole keeps turning until it lines up with the field. That is the real picture behind the formula.

tagline: Curvature creates a time delay across wavefronts
audio_script: Why does a convex lens focus parallel rays of light to a single point? It is all about time. Light travels slower inside glass than in air. The middle of a convex lens is thick, while the edges are thin. So light passing through the center is delayed the most, while light at the edges zips through quickly. To keep the light waves in phase, the wavefronts tilt inward toward the center. That geometric delay forces all the rays to meet at the focal point.

tagline: Voltage builds up as charges crowd together
audio_script: Think of a resistor as a narrow pipe and a capacitor as a flexible rubber tank. When you connect a battery, electric current pushes charge into the tank. At first, the tank is empty, so charge flows easily through the resistor. But as charge accumulates on the capacitor plates, repulsive forces build up, pushing back against incoming current. The voltage rises exponentially according to the time constant R C. When fully charged, flow stops completely.

tagline: Symmetry breaks when mass ratios differ
audio_script: Look at two masses hanging over a frictionless pulley. If both masses are equal, gravity pulls both sides evenly, creating static equilibrium. But increase one mass slightly, and gravity gains a net advantage. The total force pulling the system is the difference in weights, m two minus m one, times g. But here is what students forget: that force has to accelerate both masses together. So the net acceleration is the difference in mass divided by the total system mass.

header_title: Light Beats Metals in Whacks - Not Waves
tagline: Photons deliver energy in single packets
column28: If light were purely a continuous wave, shining brighter light on a metal would give electrons more energy until they popped out. But experiments showed something completely different: dim blue light knocks out electrons immediately, while intense red light knocks out zero. Einstein explained why: light arrives in localized quanta called photons. One photon hits one electron. If the photon energy h nu exceeds the work function phi, the electron escapes instantly.
